region: United States, college and professional football
titleEn: Why the parking lot is the first course at American football games
facts: Tailgating is a pre-game social gathering in stadium car parks, where fans eat, drink and talk around open car boots before American football games.
It grew with college football in the late nineteenth century, when supporters arrived by train or car and ate outdoors before kickoff; many universities now allocate and sell parking spots for it.
The food is shared informally, with grills, coolers and folding chairs, and some campuses set rules on open flames and alcohol.
Team colours, flags and decorated vehicles mark allegiance, and rivalry is performed as playful insult rather than hostility.
Professional teams have commercialised the practice with reserved packages, but the core event remains fan-organised.
exampleEn: On a September Saturday, a family parks at eight in the morning for an afternoon college game, grills breakfast, and walks over when the marching band passes.
qualificationEn: Tailgating is most entrenched at large college football programmes in the South and Midwest; many urban stadiums have little parking, and plenty of fans never do it.

titleEn: Chicano: how a contested name became a political identity
facts: Chicano is a name adopted by many Mexican Americans, especially in the 1960s and 1970s, to assert a distinct identity rather than assimilation.
The word's origins are debated: it may come from a Mexican pronunciation of 'Mexicano' or from earlier slang, and it was once used as an insult.
The Chicano Movement organised around farm workers' strikes, school walkouts, land rights and opposition to the Vietnam War.
It produced bilingual newspapers, art collectives and university Chicano studies departments.
Today 'Chicano' often signals political and cultural commitment, while 'Mexican American' or 'Latino' are preferred by others.
exampleEn: A high-school club stages a Day of the Dead altar and records grandparents' migration stories as a Chicano heritage project.
qualificationEn: The label is contested and regional; many Mexican Americans in Texas prefer 'Tejano' or 'Mexican American', and younger people may use 'Latine' or 'Xicanx'.

region: Navajo Nation, Arizona, New Mexico and Utah
titleEn: Navajo language and the kinship questions behind a greeting
facts: Navajo (Diné bizaad) belongs to the Na-Dené family and is spoken by roughly 170,000 people, mostly in the Navajo Nation.
It is tonal and polysynthetic: a single verb can carry information that English spreads across a whole sentence.
During the Second World War, Navajo speakers served as code talkers, using the language for military communications the United States considered unbreakable.
Kinship terms distinguish maternal and paternal relatives and specify age relations, so a greeting often establishes who is older.
Most Diné children now learn English first, and immersion schools and Navajo Nation language policy aim to reverse the shift.
exampleEn: A grandmother greets a visiting student with yáʼátʼééh, then asks which clan the student belongs to before any other question.
qualificationEn: Fluency varies by generation and community; the written orthography uses tone marks that many speakers omit in texting.

titleEn: Inuktitut syllabics and the work of keeping a language alive
facts: Inuktitut is the Inuit language of Nunavut and Nunavik, written in syllabics in most of Nunavut and in Roman letters in Nunavik and Labrador.
It is polysynthetic, building long words from many affixes, and distinguishes singular, dual and plural.
Nunavut's Official Languages Act gives Inuktitut and Inuinnaqtun official status alongside English and French.
Inuit throat singing, drum dancing and oral stories are often performed in the language at community events.
Inuktitut radio and television, plus bilingual schooling, are the main ways the language reaches young people.
exampleEn: In a hamlet shop, a teenager asks qanuippit and an elder answers with a long update about the weather and family.
qualificationEn: Dialects differ enough that Inuinnaqtun is treated separately, and Inuktitut is not the same language as Greenlandic or Inuvialuktun.

titleEn: The sugar shack and the taste of a Quebec spring
facts: A cabane à sucre is a sugarhouse where maple sap is boiled into syrup, and in Quebec many also serve large traditional meals during the spring sugaring season.
The season runs roughly from late February to April, when nights freeze and days thaw so that sap flows.
Menus typically include pea soup, baked ham, eggs, baked beans and maple taffy poured on snow.
Sugar shacks are often family farms that turned part of the operation into a seasonal restaurant, and some offer sleigh rides and music.
The phrase temps des sucres names the weeks when families and school groups make the trip.
exampleEn: In March a Montreal family drives to a cabane à sucre, eats pea soup and ham, then rolls maple taffy on snow outside.
qualificationEn: The tradition is concentrated in Quebec and neighbouring maple regions; commercial shacks differ from small family operations, and many Quebecers rarely go.

titleEn: Métis fiddling and the Red River Jig as family inheritance
facts: Métis fiddle music mixes Scottish and Irish reels, French-Canadian tunes and Indigenous rhythms, and is usually played for dancing.
The Red River Jig is the best-known tune and dance: the fiddler changes tempo while dancers perform intricate footwork in place.
Tunes were passed on through family visits, weddings and New Year's dances rather than written scores.
Many Métis communities hold fiddle contests and jigging competitions, and the music is taught at cultural camps.
The fiddle often accompanies the li jig, a social dance that brings elders and children into the same room.
exampleEn: At a community hall in Manitoba, an elder tunes a fiddle and calls the Red River Jig while teenagers take the floor.
qualificationEn: Repertoires and dance styles vary between Métis communities in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, and not every Métis family plays.

community: Kwakwakaʼwakw and other Northwest Coast nations
titleEn: The potlatch as a ceremony of giving, naming and memory
facts: A potlatch is a ceremony among Northwest Coast peoples in which a host family feeds guests, gives away goods and validates names, titles and inheritance.
It marks marriages, memorials, naming and the assumption of chiefly responsibilities, and guests witness and thereby legitimise the claims.
The Canadian government banned potlatches from 1885 to 1951, and many ceremonies continued secretly or were reshaped.
Different nations have distinct protocols; among the Kwakwakaʼwakw, dances and privileges are owned by specific families.
Today potlatches are held in big halls and can last for days, with hundreds of guests.
exampleEn: A family hosts a memorial potlatch, feeding guests and distributing blankets and household goods in the name of a late relative.
qualificationEn: Potlatch is not one uniform ceremony; the term covers different practices among many nations, and some events are closed to outsiders.

titleEn: ¿Mande? and the Mexican politeness of asking again
facts: ¿Mande? is the standard Mexican way to ask someone to repeat what they said; it comes from mande usted, literally 'command me'.
It is considered more polite than ¿qué?, which can sound abrupt, and is used with strangers, elders and customers.
In Spain the same word is rare or archaic, so its everyday use is a marker of Mexican Spanish.
The form belongs to a wider system of usted deference that shapes pronouns and verb choice.
Younger urban speakers may use ¿qué? or ¿cómo? instead, especially among friends.
exampleEn: A customer at a market stall misses the price, says ¿mande?, and the vendor repeats it patiently.
qualificationEn: Politeness norms vary by region, age and class; in parts of northern Mexico ¿mande? is less common, and some speakers consider it old-fashioned.

titleEn: Quinceañera and the rehearsed arrival of adulthood
facts: A quinceañera marks a girl's fifteenth birthday with a Catholic thanksgiving Mass, a party and often a choreographed waltz.
The birthday girl is accompanied by damas and chambelanes, friends and relatives who rehearse dances for weeks.
Families may also give a ring, a Bible or a last doll, and some take a trip instead of a party.
The celebration mixes Indigenous and Catholic elements and varies widely between countries and regions.
In the United States, quinceañera businesses provide dresses, halls, photographers and choreography.
exampleEn: A girl in Guadalajara spends Saturdays rehearsing a waltz with her cousins before the Mass and the evening party.
qualificationEn: Not every family celebrates a quinceañera, and many mark the birthday with a simple meal; some communities prefer a fiesta de quince without a church service.

titleEn: Day of the Dead and the ofrenda built at home
facts: Día de Muertos, on 1 and 2 November, is a family-centred commemoration of the dead rather than a Mexican version of Halloween.
Households build ofrendas with photographs, food, candles, marigolds and personal objects for the deceased.
Families clean graves and hold all-night vigils in cemeteries, especially in Oaxaca, Michoacán and Mixquic in Mexico City.
The holiday combines Indigenous Mesoamerican beliefs with the Catholic All Saints' and All Souls' days.
It has become a tourist attraction and a UNESCO-listed tradition, which some communities see as commercialisation.
exampleEn: A family sets up an ofrenda in the living room with their grandmother's photograph, her favourite tamales and a glass of water.
qualificationEn: Observance differs sharply by region and family; some Mexicans treat it as a public festival, others as a private religious duty, and some ignore it.

region: Jalisco, Mexico City and the Mexican diaspora
titleEn: Mariachi as a family trade rather than a stage costume
facts: Mariachi is an ensemble of violins, trumpets, guitars, vihuela and guitarrón, associated with western Mexico and especially Jalisco.
The standard line-up formed in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries from regional string bands, then moved to cities and films.
Mariachis play rancheras, sones and boleros at weddings, birthdays, funerals and serenatas.
A serenata traditionally happens outside the beloved's window, sometimes at dawn, with the musicians paid per song.
Schools in Mexico and the United States teach mariachi, and all-female ensembles have challenged the male image.
exampleEn: At a wedding in Guadalajara, a mariachi plays the couple's requested songs between courses while guests sing along.
qualificationEn: Mariachi is not a single national style; regional groups differ in instrumentation and repertoire, and many Mexicans prefer other genres.

region: Central and eastern Mexico, especially the Huasteca
titleEn: Nahuatl: the language that survived the Aztec empire
facts: Nahuatl is a Uto-Aztecan language with about 1.5 million speakers, mainly in central and eastern Mexico.
It was the lingua franca of the Aztec empire and was written in the Latin alphabet after the Spanish conquest.
Nahuatl covers a group of varieties, some mutually unintelligible; Huasteca Nahuatl is the largest.
Spanish borrowed words such as chocolate, tomato and avocado from Nahuatl.
Bilingual schools and community radio help maintain the language, but discrimination pushes many families to stop teaching it.
exampleEn: A market vendor in the Huasteca greets a regular customer in Nahuatl, then switches to Spanish when serving a tourist.
qualificationEn: The label Nahuatl hides many local varieties; official recognition and teaching differ by state, and not all ethnic Nahuas speak the language.

titleEn: Marimba and the sound of a Guatemalan town square
facts: The marimba is a wooden-key percussion instrument with resonating tubes, and it is Guatemala's national instrument.
It probably developed from African xylophone traditions and was adapted in Mesoamerica, with distinct Guatemalan and Chiapan styles.
Guatemalan marimba ensembles are usually family-based and play at fiestas, weddings and religious processions.
The double-keyboard marimba, developed in the 1890s, made chromatic playing easier.
The state promotes it as a national symbol, and it appears on school and official programmes.
exampleEn: During a patron-saint fiesta, a marimba plays in the church square while families eat and children dance.
qualificationEn: Marimba traditions differ between Guatemala, Chiapas and Colombia; not all Guatemalans listen to it, and pop music dominates radio.

region: Antigua Guatemala and the Guatemalan highlands
titleEn: Holy Week in Antigua and the making of a street carpet
facts: Holy Week in Guatemala is one of the largest public religious observances in the Americas, with processions carrying large platforms through town streets.
In Antigua Guatemala, families and brotherhoods spend hours making alfombras, coloured sawdust, flower and fruit carpets for the procession to walk over.
Processions are organised by cofradías and hermandades whose members carry the platforms in shifts, sometimes for many hours.
The observance mixes Catholic liturgy with Indigenous practices and local food traditions across the country.
It draws pilgrims and tourists, and many businesses close for the main days.
exampleEn: A family in Antigua works through the night arranging an alfombra in front of their house before the Good Friday procession arrives.
qualificationEn: Local practices differ greatly between towns, and not all Guatemalans are Catholic or observe Holy Week this way.

titleEn: Garifuna: a language and a people across the Caribbean coast
facts: The Garifuna are descendants of West and Central African, Kalinago and Arawak peoples who were deported from Saint Vincent in 1797 after resisting British colonisation.
They settled along the Caribbean coast of Honduras, Belize, Guatemala and Nicaragua, and today large communities live in New York, Los Angeles and New Orleans.
The Garifuna language belongs to the Arawakan family but contains Carib, French, Spanish and English vocabulary.
Garifuna culture is known for punta music, drumming, dance and the dügü ceremony, which honours ancestors.
UNESCO recognised Garifuna language, dance and music as a Masterpiece of Oral and Intangible Heritage in 2001.
Land pressure, migration and schooling in Spanish or English threaten language transmission.
exampleEn: In a Honduran coastal village, a family prepares food and drums for a dügü, and relatives travel from the Bronx to attend.
qualificationEn: Garifuna communities differ by country and by rural or urban setting; the language is threatened but revitalisation classes exist.

titleEn: Pupusas and the pupusería as an extension of the kitchen
facts: A pupusa is a thick maize tortilla filled with cheese, beans or pork and cooked on a griddle.
Pupusas are El Salvador's national dish and are sold in small family-run pupuserías from morning until late evening.
They are served with curtido, a lightly fermented cabbage slaw, and a thin tomato salsa.
The dish is eaten by hand; cutting it with a knife is a mild breach of custom.
Pupusa-making gives many women an independent income, since the equipment is cheap and the skills are passed down.
exampleEn: On a Sunday evening, a family queues at a neighbourhood pupusería for pupusas de queso con loroco.
qualificationEn: Fillings and sizes vary by region and family; Honduras also has its own pupusa tradition, and pupusas are common in Salvadoran diaspora communities.

titleEn: El Güegüense and the satire of colonial power in Nicaragua
facts: El Güegüense is a satirical drama from Nicaragua, performed in the town of Diriamba during the January festival of San Sebastián.
The character Güegüense, a wily merchant, uses wordplay and feigned ignorance to avoid paying taxes to Spanish colonial officials.
The play mixes Spanish and Nahuatl and has been passed down orally since the colonial period.
It is performed in the street by masked dancers and musicians as a comedy with music and dance.
UNESCO recognised El Güegüense as Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2005.
exampleEn: Every January, performers in Diriamba act out Güegüense's evasions in front of a laughing crowd.
qualificationEn: The play exists in several versions and is tied to Diriamba and the Pacific region; many Nicaraguans know it mainly from school.

region: Mexico, Cuba and the Dominican Republic
titleEn: Merienda: the afternoon pause between lunch and late dinner
facts: Merienda is a light afternoon or early-evening meal, eaten in Spain and much of Latin America, that bridges the gap between lunch and a late dinner.
It usually means coffee, tea or mate with bread, cake or fruit rather than a full meal.
In Mexico and the Caribbean the merienda often falls between five and seven in the evening, while dinner may come at nine or later.
The habit reflects a day divided around a large midday lunch and a later evening meal.
Urban work schedules and longer commutes have made the merienda more casual or skipped for some families.
exampleEn: At six in the afternoon, colleagues take a break for coffee and pan dulce from the corner bakery.
qualificationEn: The timing and size of the merienda vary by country and household; in some places the word refers to a party snack table rather than a daily pause.

titleEn: Molas and the Guna women who sew identity into cloth
facts: A mola is a hand-sewn panel made with layers of fabric, cut and stitched to reveal different colours, and worn on the front and back of a Guna woman's blouse.
Guna women in Panama and Colombia make molas using reverse appliqué and embroidery, with designs ranging from animals to geometric patterns.
Molas are a marker of Guna identity and a major source of household income through cooperatives and tourist markets.
The designs are personal and can take weeks; women often echo patterns seen on other molas while adding their own variations.
Tourism has changed the market, and some communities now sell smaller, quicker pieces alongside traditional blouses.
exampleEn: A Guna woman in Guna Yala wears a mola blouse for a community meeting and later sells a smaller panel to a visiting sailor.
qualificationEn: Molas are specific to Guna culture, not Panama as a whole; tourist pieces and art-market panels differ from the blouses worn daily.

titleEn: Baseball and the long conversation of a Cuban afternoon
facts: Baseball reached Cuba in the 1860s through Cuban students returning from the United States and became linked to anti-colonial identity.
The Cuban National Series, founded in 1961, pits provincial teams and is followed closely across the island.
Later stars defected to Major League Baseball, changing the sport's economy and the way fans follow players.
Street games are played with improvised balls and sticks, and arguments about rosters are part of daily conversation.
The US embargo has limited equipment and travel, and games often happen with sparse resources.
exampleEn: In a Havana neighbourhood, an old fan explains the previous night's pitching to a stranger within minutes.
qualificationEn: Football and basketball have grown, and not everyone follows baseball; the sport's state structure and popular practices differ sharply.

titleEn: Santería and the negotiation of saints at home
facts: Santería, or Regla de Ocha, developed in Cuba among Yoruba-speaking enslaved people and their descendants, blending West African religion with Catholicism.
Its orishas, such as Ochún, Changó and Yemayá, are honoured through offerings, drumming, song and dance.
Practitioners consult divination systems, especially the diloggún shells, and initiation creates godparent relationships.
During the colonial period, orishas were associated with Catholic saints partly to conceal the religion; today the two are often honoured side by side.
After decades of official suspicion, the religion gained more public space during the 1990s and now has followers across the Americas.
exampleEn: A client visits a santero's home for a consultation, bringing a simple offering and asking about a family problem.
qualificationEn: Santería is not one church; houses differ in rules and emphasis, and many Cubans are not practitioners.

region: Dominican Republic, Santo Domingo and Santiago
titleEn: Bachata and the neighbourhood that turned heartbreak into tempo
facts: Bachata grew in the Dominican Republic in the early twentieth century from rural string music and bolero, and was long dismissed as lower-class music.
Its lyrics often dwell on heartbreak, and the genre was nicknamed música de amargue.
Traditional bachata uses guitars, bongos and güira; modern productions add electric instruments and a faster beat.
The dance is close, with small steps and a characteristic hip movement, and is danced socially at family parties and colmadones.
UNESCO added Dominican bachata to its intangible heritage list in 2019.
exampleEn: At a Sunday family gathering, someone puts on a bachata and couples dance in the living room.
qualificationEn: Regional styles differ, and not everyone likes the genre; older traditionalists often dislike modern bachata.

titleEn: Haitian Vodou as a family obligation to the lwa
facts: Haitian Vodou is a religion with West and Central African roots that developed in Haiti under slavery and is still practised by a large share of Haitians.
It honours a creator god and many lwa, spirits who mediate between the human world and the divine.
Ceremonies involve drumming, singing, prayer and at times possession by a lwa; they are led by manbo and houngan priests.
Catholic saints and imagery have been incorporated, and many families honour both traditions.
Populist stereotypes and colonial propaganda reduced Vodou to 'voodoo', but it remains a serious religious and community practice.
Haiti officially recognised Vodou as a religion in 2003.
exampleEn: A family prepares a feast for the lwa on a feast day, inviting neighbours and drummers to the yard.
qualificationEn: Vodou has many lineages and regional forms; not all Haitians practise it, and public ceremonies and household practice can look very different.

titleEn: Haitian Creole and the grammar of a shared national language
facts: Haitian Creole (Kreyòl ayisyen) is spoken by roughly twelve million people and is one of Haiti's two official languages, alongside French.
Its vocabulary is mostly French but its grammar is West African in structure, and it is not simply broken French.
Most Haitians speak Creole as a first language, while French dominates formal education, law and much of the press.
A standardised orthography was adopted in 1979 and is used in schools and Bible translation.
Creole is used in radio, music and political speeches, and diaspora communities in the United States, Canada and the Caribbean maintain it.
exampleEn: A child in Port-au-Prince asks a neighbour sak pase and gets a long, laughing answer about the day.
qualificationEn: Spelling varies between writers, and French still carries prestige; fluency and attitudes differ between urban and rural areas.

expression.glossEn: What's up? How is it going?

titleEn: Jamaican Patois and the social rules of switching
facts: Jamaican Patois (Patwa) is an English-based creole with West African grammar, spoken by most Jamaicans alongside Standard Jamaican English.
It exists on a continuum: a speaker may move between a light creole and a deep basilect in the same conversation.
Patois was long stigmatised in schools and official settings, while it dominated music, jokes and intimate talk.
A phonetic writing system developed by linguists Frederic Cassidy and Robert Le Page in the 1960s is increasingly used online, though English spelling remains common.
Code-switching is a social skill: the same speaker may use Patois with friends and formal English with a bank clerk.
exampleEn: Two friends greet each other with wah gwaan, then switch to English when a teacher joins the group.
qualificationEn: Jamaican Patois is not standard English with an accent; class, region and context shape how much creole is used.

expression.glossEn: What's going on? How are you?

titleEn: Rastafari and the reasoning session as everyday debate
facts: Rastafari emerged in Jamaica in the 1930s, drawing on Ethiopianist Christianity and the crowning of Haile Selassie I as emperor.
Followers often regard Selassie as a divine figure, and Babylon names the oppressive system they seek to leave behind while Zion stands for Africa.
Livity, a way of living, includes an ital diet, natural hair and for some followers a rejection of alcohol and many processed foods.
Ganja is used sacramentally by many Rastas as an aid to reasoning and meditation.
The movement spread globally through reggae, Bob Marley's music and diaspora communities, and it includes several mansions or branches.
exampleEn: A group sits in a yard for a reasoning, passing a chalice and discussing scripture, Africa and current politics.
qualificationEn: Rastafari is not one organisation: practices differ by mansion, and not all followers wear dreadlocks, use ganja or eat ital.

region: Trinidad, Port of Spain and the panyards
titleEn: Steelpan and the panyard as a neighbourhood conservatory
facts: Steelpan was developed in Trinidad in the 1930s and 1940s from oil drums whose tops were hammered into tuned notes.
It grew out of the banned tamboo-bamboo percussion bands, and steel orchestras became tied to Carnival.
Bands rehearse in open yards called panyards, where players learn by ear and repetition before Panorama, the national competition.
The instrument is now played in schools, churches and orchestras worldwide, and Trinidad has declared it the national instrument.
Steelband arrangements can involve dozens of players and sections, from tenors to bass pans.
exampleEn: In the weeks before Carnival, a Port of Spain panyard fills every evening with players rehearsing their Panorama arrangement.
qualificationEn: Names and pan layouts vary between bands and islands; the instrument is also called steel drum abroad.

titleEn: Crop Over and the reinvention of a Barbadian harvest festival
facts: Crop Over is Barbados's summer festival, with roots in the harvest celebrations of the eighteenth-century sugar economy.
It was revived in 1974 as a national cultural festival after years of decline.
The season includes calypso tents, soca competitions, craft markets and the Grand Kadooment parade of costume bands.
Kadooment Day, the first Monday in August, is the climax, with bands dancing through Bridgetown.
The festival is a major tourism draw and a stage for national debate about culture and commercialism.
exampleEn: On Kadooment morning, a family wakes before dawn to finish costumes before joining their band's route through town.
qualificationEn: Practices differ from the older plantation-era festival, and not all Bajans take part; some island communities hold smaller events.

titleEn: Junkanoo and the parade built from what is at hand
facts: Junkanoo is a Bahamian parade festival held in the early hours of Boxing Day and New Year's Day.
Groups called shacks spend months making costumes from cardboard, crepe paper and wire, then compete for prizes.
The parades feature cowbells, drums, whistles and dance, and the music is created by the crowd as much as by the performers.
Its roots lie in West African festivals and in the limited holidays granted to enslaved people; the name's origin is debated.
Judging rewards theme, costume craft and the discipline of a group's rush down the parade route.
exampleEn: At two in the morning on Boxing Day, a shack's dancers line up in Nassau as drums begin and the crowd pushes forward.
qualificationEn: Celebrations differ between Nassau and the Family Islands, and commercial sponsorship has changed how groups compete.

region: Puerto Rico and the Puerto Rican diaspora
titleEn: Mofongo and the pilón at the centre of a Puerto Rican table
facts: Mofongo is a Puerto Rican dish of fried green plantains mashed with garlic, olive oil and pork crackling, often served with broth.
It is traditionally made in a wooden pilón, and the pounding gives it a dense, slightly chunky texture.
Mofongo is eaten as a main or side, often with shrimp, chicken or fish in a garlic sauce.
The dish reflects African, Spanish and Taíno influences, and plantains have been central to Caribbean cooking for centuries.
It is a standard menu item at family gatherings and roadside kiosks, and debates about the best version are common.
exampleEn: At a Sunday lunch, an aunt pounds plantains in the pilón while cousins argue about how much crackling belongs in the mix.
qualificationEn: Versions differ between Puerto Rico and the diaspora, and some families make mofongo without pork; the dish is not the same as Dominican mangú.

region: Rio de Janeiro, Bahia and nationwide
titleEn: Feijoada and the long Brazilian Saturday lunch
facts: Feijoada is a Brazilian stew of black beans and pork cuts, traditionally served on Saturdays with rice, collard greens, farofa and orange slices.
Its origin is debated: one popular story links it to enslaved people using discarded cuts, but historians also point to Portuguese bean-and-pork stews and later Brazilian adaptations.
Restaurants and families serve it at lunch, followed by long conversation and often a nap; the meal can last all afternoon.
The dish varies by region: in Bahia it may include dried meat and different spices, while Rio de Janeiro claims the classic version.
Feijoada is a social institution as much as a recipe, tied to samba, family visits and weekend hospitality.
exampleEn: On a Saturday afternoon, a Rio family serves feijoada to relatives who arrive late and stay until evening.
qualificationEn: The enslaved-origin story is popular but simplified; regional versions differ, and many Brazilians eat feijoada only occasionally.

titleEn: Capoeira and the roda as a school of improvisation
facts: Capoeira is an Afro-Brazilian practice combining dance, acrobatics, music and fighting, developed by enslaved Africans and their descendants.
It is played in a circle called the roda, where two people interact while others play berimbau, atabaque and sing.
The berimbau's rhythm sets the pace and style, and songs comment on history, struggle and everyday life.
Capoeira was criminalised in the early republic and later promoted as a national sport; today it has schools worldwide.
Teachers called mestres pass on sequences and songs orally, and students progress through belts or cordões.
exampleEn: In a Salvador academy, students form a roda, sing a call-and-response, and two players enter for a playful, fast exchange.
qualificationEn: Styles differ: Angola is slower and closer to the ground, Regional emphasises upright kicks and spectacle, and not all schools teach history the same way.

region: Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo
titleEn: The samba school and the year-long rehearsal of Carnival
facts: A samba school is a neighbourhood association that produces a Carnival parade with drummers, dancers, floats and a theme song.
Schools choose an enredo, or plot, each year, and composers compete to write the samba that the whole school will sing.
Rehearsals run for months, and the parade is judged on song, drumming, costumes, floats and the discipline of the group.
Many schools grew from favela communities and function as social clubs with classes and events year-round.
The Rio parade takes place in the Sambadrome, with each school given a strict time limit.
exampleEn: From August, a school's quadra fills on Saturdays as the bateria rehearses the year's samba and dancers learn the choreography.
qualificationEn: Carnival traditions differ between Rio, São Paulo and other cities, and not every neighbourhood has a school.

region: Rio de Janeiro, Salvador, Recife and Ouro Preto
titleEn: Brazilian Carnival and the economics of collective joy
facts: Carnival in Brazil is a national holiday period of parades, street parties and family gatherings before Lent.
Rio's samba school parades and the street blocos are different traditions: one is a judged spectacle, the other often a free, crowded street party.
Carnival has roots in Portuguese entrudo festivities and Afro-Brazilian practices, and it became a mass urban event in the twentieth century.
Cities such as Salvador, Recife and Ouro Preto have distinctive styles, from trios elétricos to frevo and maracatu.
The event is a major economic force but also a site of debates about racism, sexuality and public spending.
exampleEn: In Salvador, a bloco follows a sound truck through the streets while a crowd dances for hours in the heat.
qualificationEn: Brazilian Carnival is not one festival; practices differ by city and region, and many Brazilians avoid the crowds entirely.

region: Bahia, Rio de Janeiro and other states
titleEn: Candomblé and the terreiro as a second household
facts: Candomblé is an Afro-Brazilian religion that developed in Bahia and other regions among enslaved Africans and their descendants.
It honours orixás, divinities associated with natural forces and human activities, through offerings, drumming, dance and food.
Each terreiro, or temple, is led by a mãe or pai de santo and follows a specific nation or tradition, such as Ketu, Jeje or Angola.
Initiation is a long process, and members observe food restrictions and obligations to their orixá.
Candomblé was repressed and sometimes criminalised, but it is now recognised as a religion and a cultural heritage.
exampleEn: On a Friday night, a terreiro fills with drumming and singing as members honour their orixás in a public ceremony.
qualificationEn: Candomblé is not one uniform tradition; nations differ in language, ritual and music, and many Brazilians know it only through stereotypes.

titleEn: Jeitinho and the moral life of a Brazilian workaround
facts: Jeitinho brasileiro describes a flexible, improvised way of solving a problem, often bending a rule or finding a personal workaround.
It can be admired as creativity and mutual help, or criticised as favouritism and corruption, depending on who benefits.
The term is used in everyday situations, from queuing and bureaucracy to repairs and negotiations.
Scholars link it to a society with weak or slow formal institutions and strong personal networks.
It overlaps with malandragem, a trickster ethic, but jeitinho usually aims at a practical solution rather than a con.
exampleEn: A delivery is stuck at a depot, so a relative who knows an employee fetches it the same afternoon.
qualificationEn: The idea is a national self-description rather than a rule; many Brazilians reject it as a stereotype, and practices vary by class and region.

region: Río de la Plata and the Pampas
titleEn: Asado and the long negotiation of the Argentine grill
facts: Asado is the Argentine and Uruguayan barbecue, and it is as much a social event as a cooking method.
A grillmaster, the asador, cooks beef, sausages and offal slowly over wood or charcoal, often starting hours before guests eat.
The meal begins with a picada and ends with long conversation; rushing the meat is considered a mistake.
Sunday asado with family is common, and the asador's authority over the fire is accepted for the afternoon.
In cities, apartment balconies and shared grills substitute for the garden parrilla.
exampleEn: On a Sunday, a father starts the fire at noon while relatives arrive with salads and bread, and the first meat is served around three.
qualificationEn: Styles differ between Argentina, Uruguay and southern Brazil; not everyone can afford beef regularly, and many families grill chicken or vegetables.

titleEn: Mate and the etiquette of passing the gourd
facts: Mate is a caffeine-rich infusion of yerba mate drunk from a gourd with a metal straw, and it is central to social life in Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and southern Brazil.
One person, the cebador, pours hot water and passes the gourd in a fixed order, and each drinker finishes the cup before returning it.
Passing the mate implies trust and company; refusing it can seem cold, while saying gracias signals that you have had enough.
Sharing mate is common at work, in parks and on long drives, and the gourd travels with its drinker.
In Paraguay, the cold tereré version is everyday refreshment, especially in hot weather.
exampleEn: In a Montevideo plaza, a friend fills the gourd, passes it to a newcomer, and continues the round while talking.
qualificationEn: Rules and vocabulary vary between countries; in some settings mate is shared, in others each person keeps their own, and not everyone likes the bitter taste.

titleEn: Tango and the codes of the Buenos Aires milonga
facts: Tango developed in the working-class neighbourhoods of Buenos Aires and Montevideo in the late nineteenth century, from European and Afro-Rioplatense musical elements.
The milonga is the social dance event, with a codified etiquette: dancers ask with a cabeceo, a nod, and couples move in a line around the floor.
Traditional tango orchestras used bandoneón, violin, piano and double bass.
Tango was once considered scandalous, then became a national symbol and a global export; UNESCO lists it as intangible heritage.
Lyrics often use lunfardo slang and dwell on loss, nostalgia and the city.
exampleEn: At a Buenos Aires milonga, a man catches a woman's eye across the room, nods, and they meet on the floor for a set of three songs.
qualificationEn: Styles differ between Buenos Aires and Montevideo and between salon and stage tango; not all Argentines dance it, and young dancers often prefer nuevo tango.

titleEn: Popol Vuh and the K'iche' story of how people were made
facts: The Popol Vuh is a K'iche' Maya narrative written in the sixteenth century in the K'iche' language using Latin script, and later copied by a Dominican friar.
It recounts the creation of the world, the failures of the first humans, and the adventures of the Hero Twins, Hunahpu and Xbalanque.
The text also describes the migration and history of the K'iche' lineages before the Spanish conquest.
It survived because it was written down, and it is now read in translation in schools and studied by scholars.
The title Popol Vuh is a modern label; the text is not a pan-Maya scripture but a specific community's account.
exampleEn: A teacher in Quetzaltenango reads the Hero Twins' descent into Xibalba aloud, and students compare it with stories their grandparents tell.
qualificationEn: Translations differ substantially, and the text is specifically K'iche'; other Maya peoples have their own histories and sacred narratives.

titleEn: Ciclovía and the Sunday handover of the Bogotá street
facts: Ciclovía began in Bogotá in the 1970s and closes main roads to cars on Sunday mornings so people can cycle, walk and exercise.
The route now covers over 120 kilometres and passes through neighbourhoods of very different incomes.
It is run by the city with police, volunteers and health workers, and free exercise classes take place along the way.
The idea has spread to other Latin American and US cities, sometimes under the name open streets.
Supporters stress public health, air quality and social mixing; critics complain about traffic and cost.
exampleEn: On a Sunday morning, a family cycles from the north of Bogotá to the centre, stopping at a dance class and a fruit stall.
qualificationEn: Ciclovía is a specific Bogotá programme, not a general Colombian custom; other cities run smaller or occasional versions, and rain can cancel it.

region: Colombia's Caribbean coast and the interior
titleEn: Cumbia and the coastal rhythm that became continental
facts: Cumbia developed on Colombia's Caribbean coast from Indigenous, African and Spanish musical elements, and was originally a courtship dance.
Traditional ensembles use drums such as the tambor alegre and llamador, flutes and maracas.
Cumbia spread across Latin America in the twentieth century and was adapted into many regional styles, from Mexican cumbia sonidera to Peruvian chicha.
The dance is usually a couple dance with a shuffling step, and it is common at parties and family celebrations.
In Colombia, cumbia is a national symbol and is performed at festivals such as Barranquilla's Carnival.
exampleEn: At a family party, the DJ plays a cumbia and grandparents join the younger guests on the floor.
qualificationEn: Cumbia is not one genre; Colombian, Mexican and Peruvian versions differ in tempo, instruments and dance, and some Colombians find the term covers too much.

region: Eje Cafetero and the Andean coffee belt
titleEn: Coffee, family farms and the price of a Colombian landscape
facts: Coffee is grown mostly on small family farms in the Andean departments of Antioquia, Caldas, Quindío, Risaralda and Tolima.
The National Federation of Coffee Growers, founded in 1927, guarantees purchases and provides extension services, and its Juan Valdez campaign is widely recognised.
Harvest labour is often hired from outside the region, and pickers' families camp on farms during the season.
The Coffee Cultural Landscape was inscribed by UNESCO in 2011, recognising the landscape and culture of smallholder farming.
Coffee prices, climate change and younger people leaving for cities put pressure on the model.
exampleEn: In the harvest months, a family in the Eje Cafetero opens its home to pickers and serves meals between shifts in the field.
qualificationEn: Colombia is not the only coffee-producing country, and not all coffee is grown on family farms; the cultural landscape label covers a specific region.

titleEn: Chifa and the Chinese-Peruvian kitchen
facts: Chifa is the Peruvian Chinese restaurant tradition, named after the Cantonese phrase for eating rice and concentrated in Lima's Chinatown and neighbourhoods.
Chinese labourers arrived in Peru from the 1840s, and their descendants developed a hybrid cuisine using wok techniques with Peruvian ingredients.
Chifa dishes include arroz chaufa, tallarín saltado and sopa wantán, and the restaurants are often large, family-run and open late.
The word chifa can refer to the restaurant, the cuisine or the meal.
Peruvian-Chinese food is now present across the Americas and has influenced Peruvian national cuisine.
exampleEn: A family orders arroz chaufa and tallarín saltado at a neighbourhood chifa, sharing everything from the middle of the table.
qualificationEn: Chifa is not the same as Chinese food in China; Peruvian ingredients and local tastes changed the dishes, and there are also Japanese-Peruvian nikkei traditions.

region: Andean highlands from Ecuador to Bolivia
titleEn: Quechua and the everyday words that outlast empire
facts: Quechua is a family of languages spoken by millions of people in Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, Colombia, Argentina and Chile.
It was the language of the Inca state and remains the most widely spoken Indigenous language family in the Americas.
Varieties differ so much that a speaker from Cusco and one from Ecuador may not understand each other; Quechua is a family, not one language.
Suffixes carry information about who speaks, to whom and with what attitude, so one root can produce many social meanings.
Bilingual education and radio have supported the language, but migration and discrimination reduce transmission.
exampleEn: A market seller in Cusco greets a customer with allillanchu and continues the conversation in Quechua while weighing produce.
qualificationEn: Spelling and vocabulary vary between regions and standardisation is contested; many Quechua speakers are bilingual in Spanish, and some families no longer teach the language.

expression.glossEn: How are you? Are you well?

titleEn: Tereré and the shared cup in Paraguayan heat
facts: Tereré is cold yerba mate, drunk from a gourd or guampa through a metal straw, and it is the everyday drink of Paraguay.
The infusion is made with cold water or herbs such as mint, and it is shared in a round like hot mate.
It is especially common in the heat, at work, in the street and in casual meetings, and the equipment travels with people.
The drink is so common that social gatherings often start with it rather than coffee.
It is promoted as part of national identity, with public events celebrating it.
exampleEn: At a roadside stop outside Asunción, a family fills the guampa with cold water and passes it around while waiting for the bus.
qualificationEn: Tereré is most strongly associated with Paraguay and nearby regions, not all of Latin America; mixtures and equipment vary, and sharing has etiquette rules that differ from mate.

titleEn: Guaraní and Jopara: a language spoken between two
facts: Guaraní is an Indigenous language of the Tupi–Guaraní family and, with Spanish, an official language of Paraguay.
It is unusual in the Americas for an Indigenous language to be spoken by most of the non-Indigenous population as well.
Everyday speech often mixes Guaraní and Spanish in jopara, a fluid code-mixing that is the normal register for many Paraguayans.
Guaraní has a rich oral literature and is the language of popular songs, jokes and political rhetoric.
The 1992 constitution recognised it as official, and bilingual schooling is required, though Spanish still dominates formal institutions.
exampleEn: A bus driver in Asunción greets passengers with mba'éichapa and switches between Guaraní and Spanish as the conversation goes.
qualificationEn: Guaraní in Paraguay is not identical to the Guaraní varieties spoken in Bolivia, Brazil or Argentina, and urban vocabulary differs from rural usage.

expression.glossEn: How are you? How's it going?

titleEn: Alasitas and the economy of miniature dreams
facts: Alasitas is an Andean festival in La Paz and other Bolivian cities, held mainly in late January, in which people buy miniature objects to be blessed.
The miniatures represent things the buyer hopes for in the year: a house, a car, a university degree, money or a business.
A small figure called Ekeko, a mustachioed man carrying goods, is central to the festival, and stalls sell miniatures of every kind.
The objects are blessed by a priest, and the ritual mixes Catholic practice with Andean ideas of abundance.
The festival has expanded into a major market and a tourist event, and similar celebrations occur in Puno, Peru.
exampleEn: A student buys a miniature diploma and a tiny pile of banknotes, then takes them to be blessed before the school year starts.
qualificationEn: Alasitas is a La Paz-centred tradition with local variations; some Bolivians regard it as folk custom rather than religion, and the market is heavily commercialised.

titleEn: The cholita and the pollera as a claim to urban space
facts: The pollera is a full skirt and blouse ensemble associated with Andean women, and in Bolivia the cholita style pairs it with a bowler hat and shawl.
Cholitas are Aymara and Quechua women who wear the pollera in urban public life, especially in La Paz and El Alto.
The style was once stigmatised as rural and Indigenous, and it became a symbol of pride and political presence in the 2000s.
Cholita wrestlers, fashion shows and beauty contests have made the dress visible internationally.
Prices vary widely: a good pollera and shawl can cost as much as a month's wages, and families pass pieces between generations.
exampleEn: An El Alto market trader arrives at her stall in a layered pollera, bowler hat and shawl, and spends the first minutes arranging her skirts.
qualificationEn: The pollera is worn differently in Peru, Bolivia and Argentina, and not all Indigenous women wear it; younger women often mix it with modern clothing.

titleEn: Mapuche and the language of land and greeting
facts: The Mapuche are an Indigenous people of south-central Chile and Argentina, and Mapudungun is their language.
Mapudungun is not related to Quechua or Guaraní; it is a language isolate with its own sound system and grammar.
The greeting mari mari is widely used, and oratory and storytelling are highly valued in community meetings.
The language has been eroded by Spanish-language schooling and urban migration, and revitalisation classes now exist in both countries.
Mapuche political organisations have campaigned for land rights, recognition and language teaching, especially since the 1990s.
exampleEn: At a community gathering in Araucanía, an elder opens with a mari mari and speaks in Mapudungun before switching to Spanish for visitors.
qualificationEn: Mapuche communities are diverse, and not all Mapuche people speak Mapudungun; dialects differ between Chile and Argentina, and official recognition is uneven.

titleEn: Otavalo market and the politics of wearing identity
facts: Otavalo, in the Ecuadorian Andes, is known for its Saturday market and for Kichwa families who sell woven textiles and clothing in Ecuador and abroad.
Otavalo traders have travelled as far as Europe and North America since the 1970s, creating a transnational merchant network.
The market sells ponchos, scarves, hats and jewellery, and many stalls are run by women.
Kichwa is the local Indigenous language, and bilingual education and radio support it, though Spanish dominates commerce and schooling.
Tourism has brought income but also pressure to produce cheaper, faster goods and to perform traditional identity for buyers.
exampleEn: On a Saturday morning, a Kichwa family lays out ponchos and scarves in the Plaza de Ponchos while tour buses arrive.
qualificationEn: Otavalo is not representative of all Ecuadorian Indigenous communities; market practices differ between families, and many younger people work in other sectors.

titleEn: Candombe and the comparsa of Montevideo
facts: Candombe is an Afro-Uruguayan music and dance tradition centred on drums called tambores, played by comparsas during Carnival and at other gatherings.
The rhythm has three drum sizes, piano, repique and chico, and each has a distinct role in the groove.
Candombe developed among enslaved Africans and their descendants in Montevideo, and it was long confined to poorer neighbourhoods.
Comparsas rehearse in candombeadas in the streets of Barrio Sur and Palermo, and the sound is associated with those neighbourhoods.
UNESCO added candombe to its intangible heritage list in 2009.
exampleEn: On a Sunday afternoon, neighbours bring drums to a corner in Barrio Sur, and a comparsa forms as people join the rhythm.
qualificationEn: Candombe in Uruguay is not the same as Argentine candombe or Brazilian Candomblé, and not all Uruguayans take part; the tradition is closely tied to Afro-Uruguayan communities.

titleEn: Arepa and the rhythm of a Venezuelan day
facts: Arepas are round maize cakes, grilled or fried, eaten across Venezuela and Colombia and central to daily meals.
In Venezuela they are usually split and filled with cheese, meat or beans, and eaten at breakfast or as a snack.
The arepa is a marker of national identity in Venezuela, and areperas sell them around the clock.
Colombian arepas vary by region: thin and griddled in some areas, thick and white in others, and topped differently.
Making arepas from precooked maize flour is quick, which helped the food travel with migrants and become a diaspora staple.
exampleEn: A family in Caracas starts the day with arepas filled with cheese, made while coffee brews.
qualificationEn: Venezuelan and Colombian arepas are not the same dish, and regional styles differ widely; some families use fresh maize rather than flour.

titleEn: Mashramani and the politics of a Guyanese national festival
facts: Mashramani is Guyana's national festival on 23 February, marking the republic's founding in 1970.
The name is often glossed as celebration after hard work in an Indigenous language, and the event mixes Amerindian, African, Indian and other Guyanese traditions.
The day includes a costume parade, steelband and soca performances, calypso and a flag-raising ceremony.
Schools, ministries and community groups enter floats and costumes, and the parade moves through Georgetown.
The festival is a public holiday and an expression of national identity in a country divided by ethnic politics.
exampleEn: On 23 February, families line the streets of Georgetown to watch costumed bands and steelbands pass.
qualificationEn: Mashramani is a national, state-sponsored event, and its Indigenous name is debated; community celebrations differ from the official parade.

region: Suriname and the Surinamese diaspora in the Netherlands
titleEn: Winti and the household spirits of Suriname
facts: Winti is an Afro-Surinamese religion that developed among enslaved Africans and combines West African traditions with Christian elements.
It honours a pantheon of spirits, including the earth mother and ancestors, and ceremonies involve drumming, dance and offerings.
Winti was banned by colonial authorities and missionaries, and it remained semi-hidden for generations.
In 1971 a court case effectively decriminalised its practice, and it has since gained more public recognition.
Surinamese migrants have carried Winti to the Netherlands, where it continues in urban communities.
exampleEn: A family holds a ceremony for an ancestor, with drummers, food and a ritual specialist leading the songs.
qualificationEn: Winti is not one uniform religion; practices differ between families and regions, and many Surinamese belong to other faiths.
